name: Front raise
angleNote: Shoulder flexion: 0° = arm by your side, 90° = arm pointing forward at shoulder height, 180° = straight overhead (the overhead variant).
jointNote: Not truly one joint: the shoulder blade turns upwards on the rib cage as the arm rises, so the angle here is the whole arm against the trunk. In 12 people reaching overhead, the shoulder joint itself moved about 2.3° for every 1° of shoulder-blade rotation on the way up (2.7 on the way down), and the first 30° came mostly from the shoulder joint (about 3.7 : 1); Inman's classic figure is 2 : 1. Above about 30° a good part of the raise is the shoulder blade turning. The model treats the arm as turning about one fixed shoulder point; the shoulder-blade muscles (trapezius, serratus anterior) that turn the blade aren't analysed.
jointNoteSource: Braman JP, Engel SC, LaPrade RF, Ludewig PM (2009). In vivo assessment of scapulohumeral rhythm during unconstrained overhead reaching in asymptomatic subjects. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 18(6):960–967. doi:10.1016/j.jse.2009.02.001

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end, from de Leva's adjusted Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov table (young adult males). The forearm segment includes the hand (combined centre of mass along elbow → grip).
segments.massSource: de Leva P (1996). Adjustments to Zatsiorsky-Seluyanov's segment inertia parameters. J Biomech 29(9):1223–1230. doi:10.1016/0021-9290(95)00178-6 (Table 4, males)
segments.note: Shoulder→elbow and elbow→grip centre in metres, typical adult. The arm is modelled straight.

strengthCurve.label: Shoulder flexor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative shoulder-flexion strength vs flexion: "descending" in all three studies Kulig et al. reviewed, strongest low, with a plateau around 45–90° and a clear drop only beyond about 110°. The size of the drop across 0–90° isn't given numerically, so these values are an estimate of that shape; Mayer et al. found the isometric peak at 35–72° (men). Peak torque default: Mayer's isometric shoulder flexion, men, 68 ± 18 Nm. From 90° to 160° the drop is measured: standing isometric shoulder flexion fell almost linearly, to 56% of its 90° value at 160° (Aronis et al., Table 1); the points here are those ratios applied to the 90° value, held flat beyond 160° (not measured). Their mean at 90° was 77 Nm including the arm's own weight, above this curve's 63 Nm there; the default peak stays at Mayer's value.
strengthCurve.source: Kulig K, Andrews JG, Hay JG (1984). Human strength curves. Exerc Sport Sci Rev 12:417–466 (shape); Mayer F, Horstmann T, Röcker K, Heitkamp HC, Dickhuth HH (1994). Int J Sports Med 15:S19–S25. doi:10.1055/s-2007-1021105 (peak torque); Aronis G, Kurz M, Wimmer F, Hackl H, Angeli T, Gföhler M (2025). Maximum shoulder torque and muscle activation during standing arm flexion: reference data for biomechanical and ergonomic applications. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 11(1):20. doi:10.3390/jfmk11010020 (14 men, standing, isometric, 90–160° every 10°; Table 1 torque, Table 2 EMG)

muscles.name: Anterior deltoid
muscles.note: Main shoulder flexor. Stays fully active overhead: 95–102% of its 90° level up to 160° (Aronis et al.).
muscles.source: Campos YAC, Vianna JM, Guimarães MP, Oliveira JLD, Hernández-Mosqueira C, da Silva SF, Marchetti PH (2020). Different shoulder exercises affect the activation of deltoid portions in resistance-trained individuals. J Hum Kinet 75:5–14. doi:10.2478/hukin-2020-0033 (13 men, 60% 1RM, % of maximal isometric activation); Aronis G, Kurz M, Wimmer F, Hackl H, Angeli T, Gföhler M (2025). Maximum shoulder torque and muscle activation during standing arm flexion: reference data for biomechanical and ergonomic applications. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 11(1):20. doi:10.3390/jfmk11010020 (14 men, standing, isometric, 90–160° every 10°; Table 1 torque, Table 2 EMG)

muscles.name: Pectoralis major (clavicular head)
muscles.note: Upper chest; assists flexion in the lower and middle range. The clavicular head works with the front deltoid in flexion; inclining a press shifts the pectoral work to it (Trebs et al.). Overhead its share falls: in maximal standing flexion its EMG dropped from 69% of maximum at 90° to 20% at 160° (Aronis et al.); the weights above 90° follow that ratio.
muscles.source: Trebs AA, Brandenburg JP, Pitney WA (2010). An electromyography analysis of 3 muscles surrounding the shoulder joint during the performance of a chest press exercise at several angles. J Strength Cond Res 24(7):1925–1930. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181ddfae7 (15 men, 70% 1RM, Smith machine; values in figures only); Aronis G, Kurz M, Wimmer F, Hackl H, Angeli T, Gföhler M (2025). Maximum shoulder torque and muscle activation during standing arm flexion: reference data for biomechanical and ergonomic applications. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 11(1):20. doi:10.3390/jfmk11010020 (14 men, standing, isometric, 90–160° every 10°; Table 1 torque, Table 2 EMG)

muscles.name: Lateral deltoid
muscles.note: Helps more if the arm drifts out to the side. Overhead it works more: in maximal standing flexion its EMG rose from 88% of maximum at 90° to 109% at 150° (Aronis et al.); the weights above 90° follow that ratio.
muscles.source: Campos YAC, Vianna JM, Guimarães MP, Oliveira JLD, Hernández-Mosqueira C, da Silva SF, Marchetti PH (2020). Different shoulder exercises affect the activation of deltoid portions in resistance-trained individuals. J Hum Kinet 75:5–14. doi:10.2478/hukin-2020-0033 (13 men, 60% 1RM, % of maximal isometric activation); Aronis G, Kurz M, Wimmer F, Hackl H, Angeli T, Gföhler M (2025). Maximum shoulder torque and muscle activation during standing arm flexion: reference data for biomechanical and ergonomic applications. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 11(1):20. doi:10.3390/jfmk11010020 (14 men, standing, isometric, 90–160° every 10°; Table 1 torque, Table 2 EMG)

muscles.name: Upper trapezius
muscles.note: Rotates the shoulder blade upwards as the arm rises. In loaded raises 72–79% of maximum (Ekstrom et al., scapular plane).
muscles.source: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Soderberg GL (2003). Surface electromyographic analysis of exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 33(5):247–258. doi:10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247 (Tables 1, 3, 4: 30 adults, loaded raises in the scapular plane, % of maximal isometric activation)

muscles.name: Serratus anterior
muscles.note: Turns the shoulder blade upwards (with the trapezius) so the arm can rise forward and up; its share grows as the arm goes up, and most of the motion above shoulder height is the shoulder blade turning. The model has no shoulder blade; the weights follow EMG. Loaded raises in the scapular plane (Ekstrom et al.): serratus anterior 62% of maximum below 80° and 96% above 120°, lower trapezius 50% and 61%, upper trapezius 72% and 79%.
muscles.source: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Soderberg GL (2003). Surface electromyographic analysis of exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 33(5):247–258. doi:10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247 (Tables 1, 3, 4: 30 adults, loaded raises in the scapular plane, % of maximal isometric activation); direction from Braman JP, Engel SC, LaPrade RF, Ludewig PM (2009). In vivo assessment of scapulohumeral rhythm during unconstrained overhead reaching in asymptomatic subjects. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 18(6):960–967. doi:10.1016/j.jse.2009.02.001 (direction only)

muscles.name: Lower trapezius
muscles.note: Part of the upward-rotation pair with the serratus anterior and upper trapezius, mostly overhead. Loaded raises in the scapular plane (Ekstrom et al.): serratus anterior 62% of maximum below 80° and 96% above 120°, lower trapezius 50% and 61%, upper trapezius 72% and 79%.
muscles.source: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Soderberg GL (2003). Surface electromyographic analysis of exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 33(5):247–258. doi:10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247 (Tables 1, 3, 4: 30 adults, loaded raises in the scapular plane, % of maximal isometric activation); direction from Braman JP, Engel SC, LaPrade RF, Ludewig PM (2009). In vivo assessment of scapulohumeral rhythm during unconstrained overhead reaching in asymptomatic subjects. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 18(6):960–967. doi:10.1016/j.jse.2009.02.001 (direction only)

phases.name: Start
phases.text: Arm by your side. A dumbbell's line of action passes close to the shoulder; a cable from behind already loads the arm.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: The free-weight moment arm grows with the sine of the angle.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: Arm near horizontal: the dumbbell's moment arm is the full arm length.

phases.name: Overhead
phases.text: Above shoulder height (overhead variant): the load's lever shrinks again, and the shoulder blade turning upwards carries more of the motion.

variants.name: Standing dumbbell front raise
variants.notes: Torque = m·g·L·sin(angle): zero at the bottom, maximum at shoulder height. Same curve as the lateral raise, in a different plane.

variants.name: Cable front raise (low pulley behind)
variants.notes: Facing away from a low pulley, the cable running between your legs. It already pulls the arm back at the bottom, so the curve is flatter than with a dumbbell.

variants.name: Chest-supported incline front raise (45°)
variants.notes: Leaning face-down on a 45° bench tilts gravity relative to the body. Below 45° gravity helps raise the arm, and the torque keeps rising past shoulder height (outside this range).

variants.name: Dumbbell front raise to overhead
variants.notes: The same raise continued over the head. The load's lever (arm length × sin of the angle) peaks at shoulder height and shrinks to zero overhead, so mechanically the top half gets easier; the shoulder blade does more and more of the turning (serratus anterior, trapezius).

wger.name: Front Raises
wger.note: Checked against wger's public exercise list (id = the number in the page address).

placement.label: Elbow bend
placement.hint: 0° = arm straight. Bending the elbow folds the forearm up, in the plane of the raise, so the weight comes closer to the shoulder and the lever shrinks: at 90° of bend, with the arm horizontal, about half the torque for the same dumbbell. The biceps holds the bend (not analysed).
